chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Al-Hasan al-Attar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the 'loan' of the private part (temporary marriage). He said: 'There is no harm in it.' I said: 'But if a child is born from it?' He said: 'It belongs to the owner of the girl, unless it is stipulated otherwise.' The correct interpretation of this narration is that we should understand the questioner's inquiry about the 'loan of the private part' as a form of concession, and that his intended meaning was the temporary marriage (mut'ah) which we have previously mentioned. He called it a 'loan' because it was not a permanent contract nor permanent ownership, thus resembling a loan (ariyyah) from which the owner can reclaim it; therefore, the name 'loan' was applied to it, even though strictly speaking, its permanent use is not permissible, as indicated by the first narration.

key_terms.عَارِيَّةِ الْفَرْجِ: Loan of the private part (a term for temporary marriage)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on temporary marriage (mut'ah) and how is it distinguished from permanent marriage in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar clarifies the jurisprudential nuance between 'temporary marriage' (mut'ah) and 'al-tahlil' (a specific form of divorce to permit remarriage), interpreting the phrase 'loan of the private part' as a non-permanent, revocable union rather than permanent ownership. The Imam establishes that any offspring from such a union belongs to the woman unless explicitly stipulated otherwise, highlighting the flexibility in Shia fiqh regarding contractual conditions. This reflects the broader scholarly tradition of distinguishing between the literal terminology used in reports and their precise legal implications.
